passage:
From our parenting-class notebook, written by Tenzin, Ritu's papa.
Sunday, the neighbours came for tea. Ritu saw the chocolate box and asked for three. I said one, after lunch. She began to cry very loudly, looking at the guests between sobs. Last month her Nani gave in when this happened, and now Ritu tries it every time we have visitors. This time I knelt and said quietly, "I hear you. One, after lunch." I did not change it. She cried a while, then went to play. At lunch she ate her dal and got her one chocolate.

qa.q: How many chocolates did Ritu ask for?
qa.a: Ritu asked for three chocolates.

qa.q: Why did Ritu look at the guests between sobs?
qa.a: She hoped the crying in front of visitors would pressure her papa into saying yes, because it had worked before; she was also genuinely disappointed.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: He stayed kind and quiet, repeated the same answer and did not give in, so the loud crying did not win.

qa.q: How might the neighbours see Tenzin's calm response?
qa.a: They might feel relieved and a little impressed that the visit stayed calm, without a shouting match or a pile of chocolates.

grounding: A young child cries loudly in front of visitors to get a yes, and a parent stays kind and steady instead of rewarding the pressure.

passage: The mela was in two days, and Vasudha wanted red glass bangles. Her papa, Tarun, came in from the fields and said, "We'll see at the mela. Not new ones this month." Vasudha pushed her plate of roti away. "Then I will not eat!" She peeped at Papa. Last time Dadi had given her sweets to make her eat. Tarun only nodded. "Your roti will wait here, warm under the cloth." He ate his own food and talked about the buffalo. Vasudha's tummy grumbled. After a while, she pulled the plate back and ate every bite.

qa.q: Where did Tarun say the roti would wait?
qa.a: He said it would wait there, warm under the cloth.

qa.q: What was Vasudha hoping when she peeped at Papa?
qa.a: She hoped her threat not to eat would worry him into saying yes to the bangles, because it had worked with Dadi before; she also felt disappointed.

qa.q: What worked about Tarun's response?
qa.a: He stayed calm and kind, kept the food ready without making a fuss and did not change his answer, so the threat stopped working.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun had bought the bangles to make her eat?
qa.a: Vasudha would learn that refusing food gets her what she wants, and she would likely try it again.

grounding: A young child threatens not to eat to change a parent's no, and the parent stays kind and steady without rewarding the pressure.

passage:
Monday: Baby Tarun cried in his cot. Aditi ran over, patted his tummy and sang "twinkle, twinkle". Then she ran to the kitchen. "Mummy! Tarun needs you!" Mummy picked him up. "Thank you for telling me, Aditi."
Wednesday: Tarun cried again. Aditi patted him and fetched Mummy. She stood very tall. "I'm the big sister."
Friday: Tarun cried while Aditi was building a sand castle. She looked up. Mummy called, "I've got him, jaan. You keep building." Aditi smiled and went back to her castle.

qa.q: What song did Aditi sing to Tarun?
qa.a: Aditi sang "twinkle, twinkle" while patting his tummy.

qa.q: What does Aditi standing very tall suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt big, proud and needed, as if helping Tarun made her important in the family.

qa.q: What did Mummy do well on Friday?
qa.a: She thanked Aditi earlier but this time took care of Tarun herself, so Aditi could keep playing and be a child too. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mummy see Aditi's help?
qa.a: Mummy probably feels grateful and touched, but she also wants Aditi to enjoy her own games.

grounding: Over a week, a young girl pats her crying baby brother and fetches her mother, feels needed, and her mother thanks her but keeps the caring job for herself.

passage: The rain was so loud on the tin roof that Mummy couldn't hear the baby crying. She was in the bathroom with the tap running. Chetan dropped his toy car. His little brother's face was red. Chetan patted his back, just like Mummy did. "Shh, shh, I'm here." Then he banged on the bathroom door. "Mummy, he's crying!" Bhavna came out, hair dripping, and scooped the baby up. "Thank you, Chetan. That was kind." She kissed his head. "Next time just call me. You don't have to fix it." Chetan picked up his car and felt very tall.

qa.q: Why couldn't Mummy hear the baby crying?
qa.a: The rain was loud on the tin roof and she was in the bathroom with the tap running.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after Bhavna thanked him?
qa.a: He felt proud and big, like an important helper; he "felt very tall".

qa.q: Why was it wise for Bhavna to say "You don't have to fix it"?
qa.a: It thanked Chetan without turning him into a little parent; he can call for help and still be a child.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhavna when Chetan bangs on the door?
qa.a: She might feel startled and then grateful that her son noticed the baby and called her.

grounding: A young boy pats his crying baby brother and fetches his mother, who thanks him but tells him he does not have to fix it.

passage:
Note for Varun's teacher, from his papa, Amandeep.
Since baby Kiran came home, every time Kiran cries, I run to him. Varun then throws his spoon or climbs the cupboard, and looks straight at me. I think he feels forgotten. You may see some of this at school. This week we gave Varun a job: he brings the clean nappy when Kiran cries. After dinner we have ten minutes of "Varun time", just us and his puzzles. Last night he said, "My time!" and hugged me. We will keep going.

qa.q: What job did Varun get when Kiran cries?
qa.a: He brings the clean nappy when Kiran cries.

qa.q: Why might Varun throw his spoon and look straight at his papa?
qa.a: He feels forgotten and left out when the baby gets attention, so acting out is a way to be noticed.

qa.q: What did Amandeep try that helped Varun feel seen?
qa.a: He gave Varun a small job and a daily ten minutes of Varun time with puzzles, just the two of them.

qa.q: If you were Varun's teacher, how could this note help you?
qa.a: It explains Varun's behaviour, so the teacher can be patient and give him small moments of attention at school too.

grounding: A parent notices his older child feels forgotten when the baby cries, and responds with a small job and special daily time.

passage: Every night the baby cried and Amma, Minakshi, hurried to him with the lamp. Noor lay alone on the mat. One night she tipped over the water pot with a clang. Amma turned. "Noor!" Noor's eyes filled up. "You always go to him." Amma was quiet. Then she said, "You're right, I've been busy. Come, you hold the lamp while I rock him." Noor held it high and steady. The next evening, Amma took her up to the roof steps. "This is our time," she said, pointing at the stars. Noor leaned on her shoulder.

qa.q: What did Noor tip over with a clang?
qa.a: Noor tipped over the water pot.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she said "You always go to him"?
qa.a: She felt forgotten and hurt, left alone on the mat while the baby got all the attention.

qa.q: What two things did Minakshi do that helped Noor feel seen?
qa.a: She gave Noor the job of holding the lamp and began a special time on the roof steps together.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see the tipped water pot once Noor explains?
qa.a: She understands it as a sign that Noor feels left out, not just naughtiness, and admits she has been busy.

grounding: A young girl feels forgotten when her mother rushes to the crying baby, acts out, and her mother responds with a job and special time.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Naveen's baby brother would not stop crying. It was loud, like a siren. Naveen pressed his hands over his ears. "Make him quiet, Mummy!" His mother, Sarika, bounced the baby. "He's tired and hot. It's very noisy, hmm?" Naveen looked at the baby's tiny foot. He wanted to squeeze it hard. Instead he slid off the bench and walked to the fish tank in the corner. An orange fish swam past, quiet and slow. Naveen watched it until the crying got smaller.

qa.q: Where did Naveen walk to get away from the crying?
qa.a: He walked to the fish tank in the corner of the waiting room.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he covered his ears?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and frustrated by the loud crying, and he badly wanted it to stop.

qa.q: Which choice did Naveen make well, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He walked away to the fish tank instead of squeezing the baby's foot, which kept the baby safe and helped him calm down.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel while bouncing the crying baby?
qa.a: She might feel tired and stretched, but she understands Naveen's annoyance and names that it is very noisy.

grounding: A young boy is annoyed by his baby brother's crying, covers his ears and walks away instead of hurting the baby.

passage:
Monday: Baby Madhav screamed all through Omkar's cartoon. Omkar reached into the cot and pinched his foot. Madhav cried even harder. Papa came fast. "Omkar, no pinching. Being fed up is okay. Hurting is not." Omkar sat in the corner, cross and sorry.
Wednesday: Madhav screamed again. Omkar put his hands over his ears. "Too loud!" Papa said, "Want to take your blocks to the balcony?"
Saturday: When Madhav started crying, Omkar grabbed his blocks himself and went to the balcony. "I'm building far away," he called.

qa.q: What did Omkar do to Madhav on Monday?
qa.a: Omkar reached into the cot and pinched Madhav's foot.

qa.q: How was Omkar feeling as he sat in the corner?
qa.a: He felt cross and sorry at the same time, still annoyed by the noise but upset that he had hurt the baby.

qa.q: What did Papa say that helped Omkar learn?
qa.a: Papa told him being fed up is okay but hurting is not, and later offered the balcony so Omkar had somewhere else to go.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had called Omkar a bad boy?
qa.a: Omkar might think his annoyance itself made him bad, instead of learning that the feeling is normal and walking away is the fix.

grounding: Over a week, a young boy moves from pinching his crying baby brother to walking away when the noise annoys him.

passage: It was raining, so all the visitors squeezed into the tiny flat at once. Aunties held the baby. Uncles brought rattles and blankets. Nobody saw Darshan in the corner. "Send him back to the hospital!" he shouted. The room went quiet. His mother, Shreya, crouched down. "You feel left out and cross. That's allowed." Then she said to the visitors, "Darshan is the big brother. He's going to show you how the baby holds a finger." Darshan held out his finger. The baby grabbed it. Later, Shreya still read his bedtime story, just like always.

qa.q: What did Darshan shout?
qa.a: He shouted, "Send him back to the hospital!"

qa.q: Why did Darshan shout that?
qa.a: He felt invisible and angry, stuck in the corner while all the visitors fussed over the baby and his gifts.

qa.q: How did Shreya include Darshan instead of scolding him?
qa.a: She named his feelings, then gave him a role in front of the visitors and kept his usual bedtime story. 🤍

qa.q: How might the visitors see Darshan after Shreya speaks?
qa.a: They may notice him for the first time as the big brother and feel glad to include him.

grounding: A young boy feels invisible and jealous when visitors fuss over the new baby, and his mother accepts the feeling and includes him.

passage: The flat smelled of baby powder. Siddharth watched his father, Tushar, rock the new baby by the window. Siddharth stomped over and raised his hand to smack the baby's leg. Tushar caught his wrist gently. "I won't let you hit. You are cross. Come here." He sat on the floor with the baby in one arm and Siddharth in the other. "It's hard when a new person comes, isn't it?" Siddharth nodded into his shirt. "After his nap, you and I will go to the park. Same as every Sunday."

qa.q: What did Tushar promise for after the nap?
qa.a: He promised that he and Siddharth would go to the park, the same as every Sunday.

qa.q: How can you tell Siddharth felt jealous of the baby?
qa.a: He stomped over and raised his hand to smack the baby, then nodded that it was hard when a new person comes.

qa.q: Which choice of Tushar's worked, and why?
qa.a: He stopped the hit gently but firmly, named Siddharth's feeling and kept their Sunday park routine, so Siddharth felt included.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel holding both children on the floor?
qa.a: He may feel tired and protective of the baby, but also tender toward Siddharth's jealousy. 🙂

grounding: A young boy tries to hit the new baby out of jealousy, and his father stops it gently, accepts the feeling and keeps their routine.

passage: In the hospital ward, Gautam stood on tiptoe beside Mummy's bed. Leela lifted the blanket so he could see. His baby sister was tiny and pink. Gautam touched her hand with one finger. The fingers curled around his. "She's holding me!" he whispered, eyes wide. A nurse smiled. "Want to help? The nappies are on that shelf." Gautam ran and brought one back, holding it carefully with both hands. Later, when the nurse said only one visitor at a time, he frowned. Why did she get Mummy all night? But he still blew the baby a kiss.

qa.q: Who told Gautam where the nappies were?
qa.a: A nurse told him the nappies were on that shelf.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when the baby's fingers curled around his?
qa.a: He felt amazed and tender; he whispered with wide eyes that she was holding him.

qa.q: How could Leela help Gautam with both his love and his frown?
qa.a: She could tell him it is okay to love the baby and still feel jealous, and give him more small ways to help.

qa.q: What is it like for Leela to watch Gautam meet the baby?
qa.a: She likely feels moved and happy to see him so gentle, and aware he may also feel left out.

grounding: A young boy meets his baby sister in hospital, feels amazed and tender, helps with a nappy and also feels a flash of jealousy.

passage:
Tuesday: Zeenat stroked baby Hrithik's hand. It was softer than her dupatta. "He's so small," she breathed.
Thursday: In the morning, Zeenat brought Ammi a nappy without being asked. In the afternoon, Ammi fed Hrithik instead of playing ludo, and Zeenat stamped off. "I don't like him today!" That night she crept to the cot and patted his tummy anyway.
Sunday: Zeenat sang to Hrithik while he kicked. "Ammi, I love him and I'm cross sometimes." Ammi hugged her. "Both are okay."

qa.q: What did Zeenat bring Ammi on Thursday morning?
qa.a: Zeenat brought Ammi a nappy without being asked.

qa.q: How was Zeenat feeling on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt tender and helpful in the morning, then jealous and cross in the afternoon, yet loving again by night.

qa.q: What did Ammi say that helped Zeenat?
qa.a: Ammi told her that both loving the baby and being cross are okay, so Zeenat did not have to feel bad about mixed feelings.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Zeenat's stamping off?
qa.a: Ammi probably understands it as normal jealousy, not a lack of love, since she has seen Zeenat's care too. 🤍

grounding: Over a few days, a young girl's tender love for her new baby brother mixes with jealousy, and both feelings are accepted.

passage:
"Mummy, look at my tower!"
"Mm, lovely, beta." Mahima didn't look up; the baby was feeding.
"Mummy! Wook! Pweeti wants milk too!"
"Preeti, why are you talking like a baby?"
Preeti climbed onto the sofa and pressed against her arm. "You don't wike me now."
Mahima closed her eyes for a moment. "Oh, jaan. I'm tired, but I love you just the same. It's not your fault. When baby sleeps, you and I will have ten whole minutes. Just us. You choose."
"Tower game?"
"Tower game."

qa.q: What did Mahima promise when the baby sleeps?
qa.a: She promised Preeti ten whole minutes, just the two of them, with Preeti choosing the game.

qa.q: Why might Preeti talk like a baby and press against her mother?
qa.a: She feels pushed out and worried that her mother doesn't like her now, so she acts like the baby to get attention.

qa.q: What did Mahima do that helped Preeti?
qa.a: She admitted she was tired, said it wasn't Preeti's fault, and promised ten minutes of undivided time.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima when Preeti says "You don't wike me now"?
qa.a: It probably stings and makes her feel guilty, but it also shows her what Preeti needs.

grounding: A young girl feels pushed out by her tired, busy mother, regresses to baby talk, and her mother reassures her and promises special time.

passage:
A note from Anand's Nani to his mother, Harsha.
While you fed the baby this afternoon, I watched Anand. He followed you from room to room holding your kurta. When you shut the bedroom door, he sat outside it and sucked his thumb, which he stopped doing last year. He asked me for a bottle "like baby". I told him he is still loved, and it is nobody's fault. Tomorrow I'll hold the baby after lunch so you can have ten minutes only with Anand. He needs you more than toys right now. 🙏

qa.q: What did Anand ask Nani for?
qa.a: He asked for a bottle "like baby".

qa.q: What does Anand sucking his thumb outside the door suggest?
qa.a: He feels pushed out and anxious, and he is acting younger so he can feel close to his mother again.

qa.q: What plan did Nani make to help?
qa.a: She will hold the baby after lunch so Harsha can spend ten minutes only with Anand.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading Nani's note?
qa.a: She may feel a pang of guilt and sadness, but also grateful for the help and the clear idea.

grounding: A young boy regresses and clings while his mother is busy with the new baby, and a grandmother arranges undivided time for them.

passage:
From Francis's baby book, written by his papa, Joseph.
Today Francis watched me change his sister's nappy. He asked, "Am I not your little boy any more?" His voice was very small. I sat him on my knee and said, "You are still my big and little one. There is room for both of you." He thought for a long time. Then he fetched her rattle and shook it. "I'm the big brother, so I know the good songs," he told her. Tonight he wants to show Nana how he holds her.

qa.q: What did Francis fetch after he thought for a long time?
qa.a: He fetched his sister's rattle and shook it.

qa.q: What was Francis worried about when he asked his question?
qa.a: He was anxious that the baby had replaced him and he was no longer his papa's little boy.

qa.q: Why did Joseph's words help Francis?
qa.a: They told Francis his place in the family was safe, so his worry could turn into pride in being the big brother.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Francis sings to the baby?
qa.a: He likely feels relieved and touched that Francis now feels secure enough to be proud. 😊

grounding: A parent reassures his son that there is room for both children, and the boy's worry turns into pride as an older brother.

passage: On the mud veranda, Ishita pulled her knees to her chin while the village women cooed over the new baby. "Now you'll love him more," she mumbled to Baba. Arnab put down the fish basket and sat beside her. "You are still my big and little one. There's room for both of you, just like two birds in one nest." He put her hand on the baby's head. "He'll need you to show him the pond." Ishita sat up straighter. "I'll show him where the frogs are." She hummed to the baby all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Arnab put down before sitting beside Ishita?
qa.a: Arnab put down the fish basket.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when she mumbled to Baba?
qa.a: She felt jealous and afraid that Baba would now love the baby more than her.

qa.q: What helped Ishita's jealousy soften?
qa.a: Baba told her there was room for both children and gave her a special role, showing the baby the pond.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Ishita's humming to the baby?
qa.a: He may feel glad and proud that she now feels secure and is starting to act like a caring big sister.

grounding: A father tells his daughter there is room for both children, and her jealousy softens into pride as an older sister.

passage: The hospital corridor smelled of soap. Tenzin held his papa Deepak's hand tightly outside the ward. Everyone was going in to see the new baby. Then Dadi came out, walked straight past the flowers, and scooped Tenzin up first. "There's my special one!" she said, pressing her cheek to his. Tenzin hid his face in her shawl and smiled. Deepak laughed. "Dadi missed you most." Dadi carried Tenzin into the ward on her hip. "Now, show me your baby brother. You can tell me his name." Tenzin pointed proudly at the cot.

qa.q: Whom did Dadi scoop up first?
qa.a: Dadi scooped up Tenzin first.

qa.q: What does Tenzin hiding his face and smiling suggest?
qa.a: He felt safe, loved and important again after feeling left out while everyone went in to see the baby.

qa.q: How could other relatives follow Dadi's example?
qa.a: They could greet the older child first and give him a proud job, like telling everyone the baby's name.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Dadi's hug?
qa.a: He may feel grateful that his mother noticed Tenzin and helped him feel he still matters.

grounding: A grandmother greets the older child first at the hospital, helping him feel safe and important during the new-baby time.

passage:
Friday: Guests crowded around the new baby. Aditi sat on the stairs, chewing her plait. Papa, Ramesh, was busy pouring tea.
Saturday: Dadi arrived from the village with a bag of guavas. She put her bag down and hugged Aditi first, tight and long. "You are my special one." Aditi giggled into her sari.
Monday: Dadi and Aditi fed the ducks at the lake while the baby slept at home. "Dadi, the baby is still small," Aditi said. "I'll teach him ducks later." She skipped all the way back.

qa.q: What did Dadi bring from the village?
qa.a: Dadi brought a bag of guavas.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling on Friday on the stairs?
qa.a: She felt left out and invisible while guests crowded around the new baby and Papa was busy.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that protected Aditi from feeling replaced?
qa.a: She hugged Aditi first, called her special and took her on a duck outing just for the two of them.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel seeing Aditi skip back?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and thankful that Dadi noticed what he was too busy to see.

grounding: Over a few days, a grandmother's first hug and special time help an older child feel safe and important after a new baby arrives.

passage: At the community centre art class, Chaitanya had drawn a big blue rocket. His sister Vidya reached across for the glue and tore it in half. Chaitanya's whole body went hot. He hit her arm. Vidya howled and hit him back. The art teacher came over. "Hands are not for hitting. Chaitanya, sit on the calm mat for a bit." From the mat, Chaitanya watched Vidya rub her arm and glare at him. Later the teacher knelt beside him. "Next time, try saying, 'You broke it, I'm mad,' and call me."

qa.q: What had Chaitanya drawn?
qa.a: Chaitanya had drawn a big blue rocket.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when his rocket was torn?
qa.a: He felt so angry that his whole body went hot, and he hit Vidya before thinking.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya say next time instead of hitting?
qa.a: He could say "You broke it, I'm mad" and call the teacher, so the problem gets fixed without anyone being hurt.

qa.q: How does Vidya probably feel after being hit?
qa.a: She feels hurt and angry too, which is why she hits back and glares at her brother.

grounding: A young boy hits his sister after she tears his drawing, faces a consequence, and is taught to name his anger and get help.

passage:
Monday: Yamini spilled juice on Sarita's rainbow drawing. Sarita's fists shook and she smacked her sister's back. Yamini cried and threw a crayon at her. Amma sent them both to separate rooms. Sarita kicked the door, still hot all over.
Tuesday: Amma and Sarita practised: "You broke it, I am mad." Sarita said it loudly, stamping her foot.
Thursday: Yamini tore the corner of Sarita's new picture. Sarita's hands balled up. Then she shouted, "You tore it! I'm mad! Amma!" Amma came with the tape.

qa.q: What did Yamini spill on Monday?
qa.a: Yamini spilled juice on Sarita's rainbow drawing.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarita's anger filled her whole body?
qa.a: Her fists shook, she smacked her sister and kicked the door, still hot all over.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why was it better?
qa.a: Sarita used her words and called Amma instead of hitting, so the picture got fixed and no one was hurt. 👍

qa.q: How might Yamini feel on Monday after being smacked?
qa.a: She feels hurt and angry, so she throws a crayon back and the fight grows.

grounding: Over a few days, a young girl who hit her sister for spoiling her drawing learns to name her anger and call for help.
